1.hook: You are not starting with machine learning. You are starting with the vocabulary the courses assume you already have — and the reason lectures feel like a maths problem when they are really a reading problem.
1.rests: nothing at all — this is the beginning
1.able: read every symbol the three courses use, and say each one out loud
1.leads: Chapter 2 (the Python half) and then all of Course 1
q: What does Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>m</sup> tell a computer to do — in three parts?
x⁽²⁾, x², a<sup>[2]</sup>: what does each superscript mean?
Why does variance square the distances instead of just adding them?
(2×3) times (3×4) — legal? What shape?
Why is log(0.001) useful rather than merely different?

2.hook: Every lab in this specialization is NumPy. Not knowing what W[:, j] does is not a programming gap — it is the difference between reading the lab and watching it.
2.rests: §1.9 vectors · §1.11 matrices — the shapes have names now
2.able: read and write every line of NumPy the labs use, and read a traceback when it breaks
2.leads: Course 1, where the maths becomes code
q: [1,2] + [3,4] — Python list versus NumPy array?
(100, 4) array, .sum(axis=0) — how many numbers come back?
What does a comparison on an array return?
Why subtract a (4,) from a (100, 4), and what is that called?
Where in a traceback do you look first?

3.hook: Everything in the specialization is here in its simplest form: one feature, one straight line, a cost you can draw on paper. Nothing later is a new idea — only more of these.
3.able: build linear regression, score it with a cost function, and train it with gradient descent
3.leads: Chapter 4 (many features) and, eventually, every model in Course 2
q: What is J(w,b) measuring, and why square the errors?
Why must w and b update simultaneously?
J goes 12, 45, 380, NaN — what is wrong?
Why does the w-derivative carry an extra x⁽ⁱ⁾ and the b-derivative not?
What does convex guarantee, precisely?

4.hook: Houses have more than a size. Everything from Chapter 3 survives — it just grows a subscript, and two practical problems appear that were invisible with one feature.
4.rests: §3.5 the cost function · §3.8 gradient descent · §1.10 the dot product
4.able: train on many features, make it fast, and stop gradient descent zig-zagging
4.leads: Chapter 5, where the model itself finally changes
q: Subscript versus superscript: which is the feature and which the example?
Why is np.dot(w, x) faster than the loop that does the same arithmetic?
Sizes 300–2000 and bedrooms 1–5 — what does that do to gradient descent?
How do you tell convergence from a stalled run?
Can a linear model discover area from frontage and depth on its own?

5.hook: The first chapter where the model changes. The line is replaced, the cost is replaced — and the update rule turns out to be identical, which is not a coincidence.
5.able: build logistic regression, explain why squared error fails here, and use regularisation
5.leads: Course 2 — every network output layer is this sigmoid
q: Two reasons a straight line fails for classification.
Why is g(0) = 0.5 exactly, and what does that make the decision boundary?
Why not squared error for logistic regression?
Trick that collapses the two-case loss into one line?
λ = 0 and λ enormous — which failure is which?

6.hook: A neuron is a dot product and a squash. A layer is several of them. A network is layers in a line. That is the whole of this chapter — the rest is notation for saying which one you mean.
6.rests: §1.10 the dot product · §5.2 the sigmoid · §1.12 matrix multiplication
6.able: say what a neuron computes, count a layer's parameters, and run a network forwards
6.leads: Chapter 7, where it learns rather than just predicts
q: Layer with 3 units taking 2 inputs: outputs? parameters?
a<sub>2</sub><sup>[1]</sup> versus a<sup>[2]</sup>?
Why is forward propagation one matrix multiply per layer?
What can Sequential not build?
Is one neuron a row or a column of W?

7.hook: Course 1 built gradient descent by hand over a week. Here it is three lines — so this chapter is about everything those three lines hide.
7.rests: §5.5 the logistic loss · §6.6 forward propagation · §1.5 derivatives
7.able: train a network, choose activations, handle multiclass, and avoid the numerical trap
7.leads: Chapter 8, which is about what to do when it does not work
q: What do compile, fit and predict each correspond to from Course 1?
Why is sigmoid a poor hidden-layer activation?
Take away all activations — what can a 100-layer network compute?
Softmax: why does raising one z lower every other probability?
What does from_logits=True avoid?

8.hook: You can build models now. This chapter is the harder question, and the one practitioners come back to most: your model is bad — what do you do next?
8.able: split data honestly, read a learning curve, and name whether the problem is bias or variance
8.leads: Chapter 9, and every real project you ever run
q: Why is choosing a model on the test set a mistake?
0.5% training error, 12% test — which is it, and two fixes?
Why can more data not help a high-bias model?
10.6% error — good or bad? What must you know first?
A program that always prints “healthy” scores 99.5%. Which two metrics replace accuracy?

9.hook: A completely different shape of model — no gradient descent, no weights, no learning rate. It asks questions instead, and on spreadsheet-shaped data it often wins.
9.able: build a tree from entropy and information gain, and say when to prefer one over a network
9.leads: Course 3 — and, in practice, most tabular problems you meet
q: Bag of 3 cats and 3 dogs — entropy? All 6 cats?
Why weight each branch by its size?
Encoding ear shape as 1, 2, 3 — what have you told the model?
Regression tree: what does a leaf predict, and what replaces entropy?
Random forest versus boosting — what differs?

10.hook: The first chapter with no y at all. Nobody supplies the answer and nobody can mark it — which is unfamiliar, and is the honest situation for most data in the world.
10.rests: §1.9 vectors · §1.17 mean and variance · §1.18 the normal distribution
10.able: cluster with K-means and flag improbable examples with a Gaussian model
10.leads: Chapter 11, which learns features nobody labelled
q: Why can you not compute an accuracy for a clustering?
What single quantity do both K-means steps reduce?
k = number of points — what is the cost, and why does that matter?
Why does anomaly detection beat a classifier when anomalies are rare?
Why does multiplying per-feature probabilities catch what each alone misses?

11.hook: The chapter where the algorithm invents its own features. Nobody tells it what a romance film is; it works that out from ratings, and the features it lands on have no names at all.
11.rests: §4.1 many features · §5.2 the sigmoid · §1.10 the dot product
11.able: build collaborative filtering, handle binary labels and cold starts, and reduce dimensions with PCA
q: Why is it called collaborative?
What does mean normalisation fix, and for whom?
How do you find similar films when the features have no meaning?
Two-tower model: the single constraint on the two networks?
What must you do to data before PCA, and why?

12.hook: No right answers anywhere — only rewards that arrive late, and the problem of working out which of your last fifty actions earned them.
12.able: read the Bellman equation, and follow a deep Q-network from state to landing
12.leads: the end of the book — and the honest limits of what RL currently does
q: Why can you not treat the reward as a supervised label?
Why discount future rewards at all?
Q(s,a) uses optimal behaviour in its own definition — why is that not circular?
Why must ε-greedy explore rather than always take the best action?
Why are most RL successes in simulation?
